from pathlib import Path

from jaxcmr.helpers import find_project_root, resolve_project_path

try:
    root_path = Path(find_project_root())
except FileNotFoundError:
    root_path = Path.cwd()




Evaluate two parameter columns through the loss interface
from pathlib import Path
import json
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data, generate_trial_mask
from jaxcmr.components import context, linear_memory
from jaxcmr.components.termination import NoStopTermination
from jaxcmr.models.cmr import make_factory

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
data = load_data(resolve_project_path("data/Dupertuys2026.h5", root_path))
record = json.loads(Path(resolve_project_path("data/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo.json", root_path)).read_text())
parameters = {name: values[0] for name, values in record["fits"].items()
              if name != "subject"}
for name in ("allow_repeated_recalls", "learn_after_context_update"):
    parameters[name] = bool(parameters[name])

CMRFactory = make_factory(
    mfc_create_fn=linear_memory.init_mfc,
    mcf_create_fn=linear_memory.init_mcf,
    context_create_fn=context.init,
    termination_policy_create_fn=NoStopTermination,
)

from jaxcmr.loss.transform_sequence_likelihood import ExcludeTerminationLikelihoodLoss

mixed = generate_trial_mask(data, "data['list_type'] == 1")
trial_indices = jnp.flatnonzero(mixed)[:1]
free_names = ("encoding_drift_rate", "recall_drift_rate")
base_params = {name: value for name, value in parameters.items() if name not in free_names}
candidates = jnp.array([
    [parameters["encoding_drift_rate"], 0.2],
    [parameters["recall_drift_rate"], parameters["recall_drift_rate"]],
])

loss = ExcludeTerminationLikelihoodLoss(CMRFactory, data, features=None)
values = loss(trial_indices, base_params, free_names, candidates)
print("Parameter order:", free_names)
print("Candidate matrix shape:", candidates.shape)
print("Objective shape:", values.shape)
print("Negative log likelihoods:", values)


Parameter order: ('encoding_drift_rate', 'recall_drift_rate')
Candidate matrix shape: (2, 2)
Objective shape: (2,)
Negative log likelihoods: [13.62458774 13.05021919]


Only one mixed list is scored here to expose the interface. The first column uses the supplied fit’s parameter values; the second changes encoding drift. The returned values are not the objectives from fitting the whole experiment.
The underlying likelihood also exposes event probabilities. Setting masked probabilities to one makes their contribution -log(1) = 0.


Connect the event probabilities and mask to the returned NLL
from jaxcmr.helpers import log_likelihood
from jaxcmr.loss.transform_sequence_likelihood import (
    MemorySearchLikelihoodLoss, mask_trailing_terminations,
)

likelihood = MemorySearchLikelihoodLoss(
    CMRFactory, data, features=None,
    mask_likelihoods=mask_trailing_terminations,
)
row = trial_indices[0]
probabilities = likelihood.predict_trial(row, parameters)
include = mask_trailing_terminations(data["recalls"][row])
event_nll = log_likelihood(jnp.where(include, probabilities, 1.0))
print("Included event probabilities:", probabilities[include])
print("Included events:", int(include.sum()))
print("NLL from event probabilities:", float(event_nll))
print("NLL from the loss call:", float(values[0]))


Included event probabilities: [0.13703638 0.04187474 0.08562368 0.19103804 0.0785633  0.16413277]
Included events: 6
NLL from event probabilities: 13.624587741452169
NLL from the loss call: 13.62458774145214


Despite its name, jaxcmr.helpers.log_likelihood() returns negative summed log likelihood. The mask selects the positive recall events; it does not define a new response sequence.

title: Loss Functions
text:
Behavioral-summary objectives
jaxcmr.loss.mse.make_factory() binds named RecallAnalysisFn callbacks into a loss class with the same fitting interface. It compares observed and simulated summaries rather than assigning a likelihood to each recorded response. Recall Analyses shows the callback contract and an adapter using the existing SPC calculation.
Its weights, scales and reduction determine how summary discrepancies contribute to the objective. Such a value is not NLL and cannot be put into an AIC formula. JAX-compatible simulation also does not by itself provide useful pathwise gradients through discrete recall samples.

title: Loss Functions
text:
Preparing a fixed selection
PreparableLossFn is an optional capability used by fitting adapters to prepare observations before JIT compilation. An ordinary loss need only implement LossFn.
Declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class PreparableLossFn(LossFn, Protocol):
    def prepare_trials(
        self, trial_indices: Integer[Array, " trials"]
    ) -> PreparedLossFn: ...
The returned PreparedLossFn takes (base_params, free_param_names, x) and returns the same candidate-wise objectives. The selected trials are already bound, including their order and multiplicity. Each prepared callable must retain its own selection. BatchPreparableLossFn extends this to several selections so implementations can share compatible preparation work.


Evaluate the same candidates with the selected trials already bound
prepared = loss.prepare_trials(trial_indices)
prepared(base_params, free_names, candidates)


Array([13.62458774, 13.05021919], dtype=float64)


The prepared call represents the same objective. Preparation is a capability of the implementation, not a change in the scientific quantity being fitted. Fitting Procedures explains how fitters consume these losses; the fitting template carries out a full run.

title: Model Evaluation
text: Evaluation uses datasets, parameter values and fit records already produced by the library. There is no single evaluation protocol: each comparison requires the representation and assumptions of the helper being used.

title: Model Evaluation
text:
Which objects answer which questions?



Question
Library inputs and operations
Complete procedure




Does the model reproduce a behavioral pattern?
Observed and simulated RecallDataset objects passed to the same analysis and plotting functions, such as plot_spc().
Simulation


What changes when a parameter changes?
Shared study inputs, a fixed model configuration and deliberate parameter interventions followed by simulation and analysis.
Parameter exploration


How do likelihood fits compare?
Compatible named fit records passed to comparison helpers in jaxcmr.summarize.
Model comparison



A behavioral match, an intervention and a likelihood comparison answer different questions. In particular, forced agreement with the observed recall length is not evidence that a model predicts when recall stops.

title: Model Evaluation
section: Fit-record conventions at the comparison boundary
text:
Fit-record conventions at the comparison boundary
FitResult provides parameter roles, objective values and row identifiers. Comparison helpers additionally use a name. The templates record the data selection, model configuration and objective needed to establish comparability.
Before comparing likelihood scores, establish that the records concern the same observations, included events and likelihood definition. Check whether parameters were pooled or independently fitted and how many values were estimated. A lower discrepancy loss cannot be substituted for NLL merely because both appear in a field named fitness.
The supplied source-only and broader eCMR records are pooled fits to the same all-condition selection with the same termination-excluded objective and stopping policy. Their emotional modulation differs in whether it also acts on temporal context. Each has ten free parameters and one pooled fit row.
Both supplied eCMR fits learn before context updating, fix emotional encoding drift at 1 and tie emotional recall drift to temporal recall drift. They omit the legacy emotion_drift_rate. Historical fits also require their original context equations and parameter interpretations; a shared import path alone does not identify that behavior.

title: Model Evaluation
text:
Compare summed negative log likelihoods
jaxcmr.summarize.calculate_aic() accepts records containing name, free and fitness, and returns a DataFrame sorted by AIC. Each fitness entry must be a summed negative log likelihood for one fitted parameter set:
\[\mathrm{AIC} = 2k + 2\,\mathrm{NLL}.\]
These saved fits already contain NLL and can be supplied directly. A pooled fit incurs one parameter penalty. Independently fitted participant rows incur one penalty each, and their identifiers must match across models.


Calculate AIC directly from the saved NLL records
from jaxcmr.summarize import calculate_aic

calculate_aic(records)









Model
AIC




1
Broader eCMR
14348.715746


0
Source-only eCMR
14358.852540







The supplied source-only and broader fits have NLLs 7169.426 and 7164.358, respectively. Their AIC difference is 10.137, favoring broader eCMR. The within-model differences between the two three-restart seed sets are 0.005 and 0.049 NLL units. The ranking is the same in both seed sets.
The result is a library-produced table. Lower AIC is preferred within this comparison; it does not establish a unique explanation of the experiment. Each model contributes one pooled parameter set, so len(free) is the parameter count for that row. calculate_aic_weights() uses the same NLL convention and parameter penalties as calculate_aic().
Participant-wise comparisons align rows by subject identifier and require finite scores for the same participant set. A pooled row is not a sample of independent participant estimates. Mean-difference helpers return the mean and interval half-width; median-difference helpers return the median and the actual bootstrap lower and upper endpoints.
calculate_bic_scores(results, n_obs) and the AICc helpers require positive observation counts for each fitted parameter row. Counts follow the first record’s original participant order; the library aligns them with the scores. Specify the scientific counting unit and selection explicitly. A scalar count is valid only for one fitted row; AICc requires each count to exceed k + 1.
floor_nested_fitness(raw_results, nesting_pairs) returns separate comparison records and an adjustment table without changing the raw fits. Label adjusted scores and save the adjustment table beside them. Keep raw fits for parameter summaries, simulations and held-out evaluation: an adjusted score is not a newly optimized parameter set. The helper trusts the declared nesting relationships.
Bayesian model selection uses an AIC/AICc-based evidence approximation over participant fits. A pooled row cannot supply participant-level inference; failure to converge raises an error rather than returning a result.

title: Model Evaluation
text:
Experimental cross-validation functionality
jaxcmr.experimental.cross_validation contains an experimental driver, with CVResult describing fold-specific fits, participant identifiers, training scores and held-out scores. The current driver mixes pooled fitting with participant-level scoring and can return incorrect held-out scores; it is not ready for scientific use. A held-out comparison requires an appropriate split, fitting only the training observations and evaluating the held-out observations under the chosen objective. It is a different procedure from comparing in-sample AIC values.
See Fitting Procedures for result structure and the model comparison template for the full pooled comparison. These interfaces organize the evidence; selecting a scientifically meaningful comparison remains part of the research design.

title: Model Components
text: Components provide the state representations and operations that a model combines. In CMR, item-to-context memory cues a context representation, context-to-item memory supports retrieval, and a termination policy supplies a stopping probability. The model determines when and how to use them.

title: Model Components
Model Components
section: Creators supply components to a model
text:
Creators supply components to a model
Models need fresh components with compatible dimensions and parameters. Creator functions provide these objects when a model is constructed.
Declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class ContextCreateFn(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, item_count: int) -> Context: ...
Declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class MemoryCreateFn(Protocol):
    def __call__(
        self,
        list_length: int,
        parameters: Mapping[str, Float_],
        context: Context,
    ) -> Memory: ...
Declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class TerminationPolicyCreateFn[ModelT](Protocol):
    def __call__(
        self, list_length: int, parameters: Mapping[str, Float_]
    ) -> TerminationPolicy[ModelT]: ...
Ordinary CMR’s make_factory() accepts four such callables:








Factory argument
Existing implementation used here
Role




context_create_fn
context.init
Construct temporal context.


mfc_create_fn
linear_memory.init_mfc
Construct item-to-context memory.


mcf_create_fn
linear_memory.init_mcf
Construct context-to-item memory.


termination_policy_create_fn
NoStopTermination
Construct the stopping policy.



A compatible function or callable class can occupy one of these arguments. Each memory creator returns one memory with the appropriate direction and dimensions. Changing a creator changes that component’s implementation; the model still owns its event ordering, parameter interpretation and composition rules. Other models may expose different configuration choices.

mixed = generate_trial_mask(data, "data['list_type'] == 1")
trial_index = int(jnp.flatnonzero(mixed)[0])
initial = factory.create_trial_model(trial_index, parameters)
print("Context:", type(initial.context).__name__, initial.context.state.shape)
print("Item-to-context memory:", type(initial.mfc).__name__, initial.mfc.state.shape)
print("Context-to-item memory:", type(initial.mcf).__name__, initial.mcf.state.shape)
print("Termination:", type(initial.termination_policy).__name__)


Context: TemporalContext (13,)
Item-to-context memory: LinearMemory (12, 13)
Context-to-item memory: LinearMemory (13, 12)
Termination: NoStopTermination

title: Model Components
section: What the model does with them
text:
What the model does with them
For a CMR study event, item-to-context memory is probed with the item pattern. Context integrates that input using encoding drift. The model then updates both associative memories; learn_after_context_update determines which context state is used for learning. During retrieval, context-to-item memory supplies item activations and the termination policy supplies stopping support. Those steps belong to CMR’s composition, not to Context or Memory on their own.


Display the context after CMR processes one study event
from IPython.display import display

updated = initial.experience(data["pres_itemnos"][trial_index, 0])
print("Original study count:", int(initial.study_index))
print("Updated study count:", int(updated.study_index))
print("Context changed:", not bool(jnp.allclose(
    initial.context.state, updated.context.state
)))
display(updated.context)


Original study count: 0
Updated study count: 1
Context changed: True





The figure uses the context object’s built-in notebook display. It shows the representation after one update; the original model retains its earlier state. A compatible replacement must satisfy the required dimensions, functional update behavior and JAX operations, as well as the protocol’s named methods. A termination policy additionally needs the attributes of the model or view passed to it.
See Memory Search Models for the enclosing lifecycle and the parameter exploration template for changing parameters within a fixed model configuration.

title: Library Guide
text: This guide explains JAXCMR’s data structures, interfaces and conventions: what each part receives, what it returns and where another part uses it. It also identifies entry points for supplying compatible functions or implementations. The Templates assemble these parts into complete research procedures.

title: Library Guide
text:
How the interfaces connect






flowchart TB
    D["RecallDataset"] --> F["MemorySearchModelFactory"]
    F --> M["MemorySearch"]
    C["Context · Memory · TerminationPolicy"] --> M
    D --> L["LossFn"]
    M -->|event probabilities| L
    M --> S["TrialSimulator"]
    S --> SD["Simulated RecallDataset"]
    D --> A["Recall analyses"]
    SD --> A
    A -. "RecallAnalysisFn callback" .-> L
    L --> O["FittingAlgorithm"]
    O --> R["FitResult"]
    R -->|assigned parameters| S
    R --> E["Evaluation helpers"]
    A --> E






A model factory creates a model for an experiment and parameter values. Likelihood calculations follow recorded responses through that model; simulation samples new responses. Both observed and simulated datasets can enter recall analyses. A compatible analysis callback can also supply the summary used by a behavioral objective. Fitters search parameter values using a loss and return records for subsequent simulation and evaluation.
Simulation can use hand-chosen parameters without a fit. Analysis can describe observations without a model. These are connected interfaces, not a mandatory sequence of steps.

title: Library Guide
text:
The structures and entry points



Page
Structure or convention
Where it connects




Data
RecallDataset, coding, alignment and storage
Dataset analyses, factories, losses, fitters and simulation.


Recall Analyses
Array/dataset functions, aggregation, plotting and RecallAnalysisFn
Descriptive results and callbacks supplied to summary-based losses.


Memory Search Models
MemorySearch and MemorySearchModelFactory
Event calculations through model_factory_cls in losses and simulation.


Model Components
Context, Memory, termination policies and creators
Component arguments accepted by model factories.


Loss Functions
LossFn, event masks and optional preparation
The objective supplied through a fitter’s loss_fn_cls.


Fitting Procedures
FittingAlgorithm, parameter roles and FitResult
Optimization and records used by later procedures.


Data Simulation
TrialSimulator, participant assignment and replications
A simulate_trial_fn callback inside dataset simulation.


Model Evaluation
Comparable datasets, fit records and objective conventions
Behavioral and likelihood-based comparison helpers.

title: Library Guide
text:
What a protocol provides
A Python Protocol describes the attributes and methods a consumer expects. A compatible implementation need not inherit from that protocol. For a callable protocol such as RecallAnalysisFn, an ordinary function with the specified arguments and behavior can be passed directly to its consumer. The analysis callback example shows this connection using an existing SPC calculation.
Signatures alone are not enough: array dimensions, item coding, parameter order and JAX-compatible operations also determine whether implementations work together. Each topic explains these responsibilities alongside the relevant declaration. Examples illustrate one connection at a time.
RecallDataset and FitResult are dictionary types, not protocols. They describe fields and alignment, without being comprehensive runtime validators. Other conventions, such as template-added provenance or objective signs expected by comparison helpers, are established by the procedures that produce and consume the records.

title: Library Guide
text:
Configuring a reusable procedure
Template notebooks separate literal settings from the Python objects constructed from them:

A tagged parameters cell holds paths, selections, parameter values, import names and output locations. Parameterized execution can replace these literals for another run.
Setup imports implementations and constructs factories, masks and other derived objects from those settings.
The procedure produces outputs and retains the effective settings.

Independent executions need separate output locations. Changes to fit parameters or simulation settings require corresponding new simulation outputs. The Templates explain parameterized execution and provide complete procedures; this guide describes the structures they connect.

title: Library Guide
text:
Using the illustrations
The topic notebooks retain small executed examples using the existing war-photo-recall observations and supplied fits. Their protocol declarations are visible; expand a labeled code block to inspect an executable example. To rerun one, use Download notebook and place it beside the shared data/ folder from the Templates downloads. The homepage gives the installation command.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Follow the war-photo-recall data through analysis, fitting, simulation and comparison. The first sections identify the settings and outputs in each template; the final section executes the same sequence with Papermill, including a separate fitting run for each model. It reuses the supplied completed fits by default.
Use the repository and environment from Local setup with VS Code. Open this notebook in that environment. The repository contains the observations and completed fits; no lab-drive files are needed. For preparing your own inputs, start with Preparing data for JAXCMR.
1 — Configure the tutorial work units
project_root = None  # The JAXCMR checkout; set explicitly when working elsewhere.
output_dir = "results/tutorial/model-comparison"
data_path = "data/Dupertuys2026.h5"

fit_sources = {
    "CMR": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo.json",
    "eCMR_source_only": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_eCMR_source_only.json",
    "eCMR_broad": "data/fits/Dupertuys2026_eCMR_broad.json",
}
model_labels = {
    "CMR": "CMR",
    "eCMR_source_only": "Source-only eCMR",
    "eCMR_broad": "Broader eCMR",
}
redo_fits = False  # True launches the full recorded optimization settings.
experiment_count = 10
simulation_seed = 1
trial_queries = ["data['list_type'] == 1", "data['list_type'] == 2", "data['list_type'] == 3"]
labels = ["Mixed", "Pure emotional", "Pure neutral"]

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Describe observed recall
Open Serial position curves. In its parameter cell, set data_paths = ["data/Dupertuys2026.h5"], data_labels = ["Observed"] and output_dir = "results/tutorial/model-comparison/observed". Leave the single-input override data_path unset. Retain the three trial_queries and matching labels shown above.
Run the notebook. It reports 491 complete lists from 123 participants, excluding the one padded study list, and produces one condition panel per query. The saved figure is observed/spc.png beneath this tutorial’s output folder. The vertical axis describes recall probability at each study position; the curve alone does not identify a memory mechanism.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Inspect a fitted model
Open Fitting models. Its first cell collects the observation selection, model specifications, fixed/free parameters, optimizer and output settings. The three supplied specifications fit all 492 lists with pooled parameters; the analysis selection for complete lists does not change the fitting selection.







Setting
Meaning in this example




model_configs
CMR, source-only eCMR and broader eCMR; use a one-entry dictionary for one model per job.


parameters["fixed"] and parameters["free"] inside each model
Fixed values and bounds for fitted values.


fit_alg_path, fit_hyperparams
Optimizer and search settings, separate from model parameters.


redo_fits = False
Load a compatible result if it exists; a missing result would still start fitting.


redo_sims = False, redo_figures = False
Run fitting/objective inspection only.



The Papermill cells below place copies of the supplied fits at the expected paths before executing fitting. They display fitted parameters and independently recalculated objectives. Expected NLLs are approximately 7202.029 (CMR), 7169.426 (source-only) and 7164.358 (broader eCMR). Each fit estimates one parameter set across all participants.
To start new fits, choose a new output_dir and set this tour’s redo_fits = True. That uses the full recorded SciPy DE settings: 1,000 generations, population multiplier 15 and three restarts, with the recorded bounds and seeds. It can take substantially longer than inspecting saved fits. For different scientific specifications, edit the per-job model_configs passed to fitting and use a new output directory.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Generate responses from the fits
Open Simulating from saved fits. Supply fitting’s printed fit_paths, set experiment_count = 10 and simulation_seed = 1, and choose a simulation_dir. The sequence below uses a distinct folder for each model and sets redo_sims = False, allowing matching responses to be reused on a later run.
The first run generates 4,920 response rows per model: ten repetitions of each of the 492 lists, retaining the original 123 participant IDs and list conditions. Each .h5 response file has a .json file recording its model parameters, selected rows, seed and repetitions. These simulations impose observed recall lengths; matching recall counts are not a successful prediction of stopping behavior.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Compare observed and simulated recall
Return to SPC. Supply the observation file followed by simulation’s printed response paths as data_paths, with matching data_labels. Use the same condition queries and complete-list selection. Simulated repetitions stay grouped under the original participant IDs when summarizing behavior.
The sequence below writes predictions/spc.png: each condition panel compares observations with all three models. Other analysis templates can read these same saved response files without fitting or simulating again.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Compare models
Open Comparing pooled model fits. Supply the same named fit_paths and simulation_paths. The notebook checks that the models use matching observations, objectives and stopping rules, recalculates likelihoods, and reports NLL, parameter counts, AIC, ΔAIC and search histories alongside behavioral comparisons.
The expected parameter counts are 9, 10 and 10. Lower AIC is better within this comparison, but its interpretation depends on the fitted specifications and optimization quality; these pooled results are not independent participant-level estimates. The saved table is comparison/pooled_model_comparison.csv.
For supported statistical examples, see category recall rate for paired participant contrasts and distance rank for tests against chance. Use participant summaries as the sampling units; simulation repetitions are not additional participants.

title: From data to model comparison
text:
Sequence the templates with Papermill
Papermill executes a notebook with a parameter dictionary and saves the executed copy. Its parameter injection occurs immediately after the tagged parameters cell, before paths, masks and models are constructed. The templates are already tagged, and Papermill is included in uv sync.
The following cells form an ordinary Python script, kept here in the notebook: import packages, prepare work units, then call pm.execute_notebook in the required order. Each fitting call receives a different one-entry model_configs dictionary. Shared memory between notebooks is unnecessary: paths identify the saved products passed to the next call. The python3 kernel must be the project’s environment, as in Local setup with VS Code.


2 — Import the sequencing and display tools
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

from IPython.display import Image, display
import papermill as pm
from tabulate import tabulate

from jaxcmr.helpers import find_project_root, resolve_project_path




3 — Resolve templates and the executed-notebook folder
if project_root is not None:
    root_path = resolve_project_path(project_root, Path.cwd())
else:
    try:
        root_path = Path(find_project_root())
    except FileNotFoundError:
        root_path = Path.cwd()
output_path = resolve_project_path(output_dir, root_path)
output_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
template_path = root_path / "templates"
if not (template_path / "fitting.ipynb").is_file():
    raise FileNotFoundError("Set project_root to the JAXCMR checkout from Local setup with VS Code.")
executed_path = output_path / "executed"
executed_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
observation_path = resolve_project_path(data_path, root_path)
execution_options = {"kernel_name": "python3", "cwd": str(root_path), "progress_bar": False}
analysis_parameters = {
    "project_root": str(root_path),
    "trial_queries": trial_queries,
    "labels": labels,
}




4 — Run the observed-data analysis
pm.execute_notebook(
    str(template_path / "spc.ipynb"), str(executed_path / "observed_spc.ipynb"),
    parameters={
        **analysis_parameters,
        "data_paths": [str(observation_path)], "data_labels": ["Observed"],
        "output_dir": str(output_path / "observed"),
    },
    **execution_options,
)
display(Image(filename=str(output_path / "observed" / "spc.png")))









The work-unit preparation below reads the exact specifications from the supplied fit records. It copies results into this run’s folder and supplies the cohort metadata omitted by the older records, using their recorded cohort indices. Original inputs are left unchanged; existing working results are not replaced.


5 — Prepare a separate fitting work unit for each model
fit_jobs = []
for model_name, source in fit_sources.items():
    fit_record = json.loads(resolve_project_path(source, root_path).read_text())
    fit_record["fit_configuration"].setdefault(
        "cohort_trial_indices", fit_record["cohort_trial_indices"]
    )
    job_path = output_path / model_name
    fit_directory = job_path / "fits"
    fit_directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fit_path = fit_directory / f"{fit_record['name']}.json"
    if not redo_fits and not fit_path.exists():
        fit_path.write_text(json.dumps(fit_record, indent=2) + "\n")

    search = fit_record["fit_configuration"]["search_settings"]
    model_spec = {
        "label": model_labels[model_name],
        "model_factory": fit_record["model_factory"],
        "components": fit_record["components"],
        "parameters": fit_record["fit_configuration"]["parameters"],
        "seed": search["seed"], "output_stem": fit_record["name"],
        "embedding_path": fit_record["embedding_path"],
        "emotion_feature_path": fit_record["emotion_feature_path"],
        "feature_column": fit_record["feature_column"],
        "concat_features": fit_record["concat_features"],
    }
    fit_jobs.append({
        "name": model_name, "directory": job_path, "fit_path": fit_path,
        "model_configs": {model_name: model_spec},
        "fit_alg_path": fit_record["fit_algorithm"],
        "fit_hyperparams": {key: value for key, value in search.items() if key not in {"seed", "bounds"}},
        "loss_fn_path": fit_record["loss_function"],
        "sim_alg_path": fit_record["simulation_function"],
        "trial_query": fit_record["trial_query"],
    })
print("Fitting work units:", [job["name"] for job in fit_jobs])


Fitting work units: ['CMR', 'eCMR_source_only', 'eCMR_broad']




6 — Execute the same fitting template once per model
fit_paths = {}
for job in fit_jobs:
    model_name = job["name"]
    pm.execute_notebook(
        str(template_path / "fitting.ipynb"),
        str(executed_path / f"fit_{model_name}.ipynb"),
        parameters={
            "project_root": str(root_path), "data_path": str(observation_path),
            "model_configs": job["model_configs"],
            "fit_alg_path": job["fit_alg_path"], "fit_hyperparams": job["fit_hyperparams"],
            "loss_fn_path": job["loss_fn_path"], "sim_alg_path": job["sim_alg_path"],
            "trial_query": job["trial_query"], "pooled": True,
            "output_dir": str(job["directory"]), "fit_dir": str(job["fit_path"].parent),
            "redo_fits": redo_fits, "redo_sims": False, "redo_figures": False,
        },
        **execution_options,
    )
    fit_paths[model_name] = str(job["fit_path"])
    fitted = json.loads(job["fit_path"].read_text())
    print(model_labels[model_name], "— saved NLL:", fitted["fitness"][0])


CMR — saved NLL: 7202.029122199305


Source-only eCMR — saved NLL: 7169.426270173915
Broader eCMR — saved NLL: 7164.357873171088




7 — Simulate from each completed fitting work unit
simulation_paths = {}
for job in fit_jobs:
    model_name = job["name"]
    simulation_directory = job["directory"] / "simulations"
    pm.execute_notebook(
        str(template_path / "simulation.ipynb"),
        str(executed_path / f"simulate_{model_name}.ipynb"),
        parameters={
            "project_root": str(root_path), "data_path": str(observation_path),
            "fit_paths": {model_name: fit_paths[model_name]},
            "model_labels": model_labels,
            "output_dir": str(job["directory"] / "simulation"),
            "simulation_dir": str(simulation_directory),
            "experiment_count": experiment_count, "simulation_seed": simulation_seed,
            "redo_sims": False, "redo_figures": False,
        },
        **execution_options,
    )
    fitted = json.loads(Path(fit_paths[model_name]).read_text())
    simulation_paths[model_name] = str(simulation_directory / f"{fitted['name']}.h5")
print("Simulation files prepared for:", list(simulation_paths))


Simulation files prepared for: ['CMR', 'eCMR_source_only', 'eCMR_broad']




8 — Run SPC on the observations and saved model responses
pm.execute_notebook(
    str(template_path / "spc.ipynb"), str(executed_path / "predicted_spc.ipynb"),
    parameters={
        **analysis_parameters,
        "data_paths": [str(observation_path), *simulation_paths.values()],
        "data_labels": ["Observed", *[model_labels[name] for name in simulation_paths]],
        "output_dir": str(output_path / "predictions"),
    },
    **execution_options,
)
display(Image(filename=str(output_path / "predictions" / "spc.png")))











9 — Compare the same fits and responses and display their scores
pm.execute_notebook(
    str(template_path / "model_comparison.ipynb"),
    str(executed_path / "model_comparison.ipynb"),
    parameters={
        "project_root": str(root_path), "data_path": str(observation_path),
        "fit_paths": fit_paths, "simulation_paths": simulation_paths,
        "model_labels": model_labels, "output_dir": str(output_path / "comparison"),
    },
    **execution_options,
)
with (output_path / "comparison" / "pooled_model_comparison.csv").open(newline="") as stream:
    comparison_rows = list(csv.DictReader(stream))
print(tabulate(comparison_rows, headers="keys", floatfmt=".3f"))


Model               Free parameters    Negative log likelihood        AIC    Delta AIC
----------------  -----------------  -------------------------  ---------  -----------
CMR                               9                   7202.029  14422.058       73.342
Source-only eCMR                 10                   7169.426  14358.853       10.137
Broader eCMR                     10                   7164.358  14348.716        0.000


Executed notebooks are under output_dir/executed; fit records, simulated responses, figures and summary tables remain in their named result folders. Papermill stops on an execution error, so a failed fitting job prevents the later comparison from silently continuing.
For cluster work, prepare one parameter dictionary and a distinct output notebook/path per work unit, then submit those jobs through your scheduler. Only launch the combined analyses after all required fits and simulations finish. Papermill supplies parameter injection and execution; it does not schedule cluster jobs.

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
Use VS Code to work with notebooks and files on a Slurm cluster. Your computer displays the editor; the cluster stores your research project and runs Python. You do not need Python installed locally.
A cluster is a collection of shared computers. Clusters provide resources for work that exceeds your computer’s capacity and for running independent jobs simultaneously. This guide prepares an interactive workspace for developing and checking your work. For unattended execution and multiple independent runs, continue with Run batches of notebooks unattended on Slurm. Requesting more CPUs does not automatically make a calculation faster.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
Where the work happens







Location
Role




Your computer
Displays VS Code and connects to the cluster


Login node
Provides access to files and lets you prepare and submit work


Compute node
Runs calculations using resources allocated by Slurm



A node is a computer in the cluster. Login nodes are shared access points, so substantial calculations belong on compute nodes. Slurm manages access: you request resources, and it starts your work when suitable resources are available.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
Before you begin
You need a cluster account and the following details from your institution:







Information
What you need it for




Login address and username
Connecting to the cluster


Authentication requirements
Any VPN, password, authentication app, or SSH key needed to sign in


Project storage location
Keeping code, installed software, and results


Slurm account
Selecting the research allocation charged for computing use


CPU partition
Selecting a permitted group of compute nodes


Supported VS Code access method
Connecting the editor to allocated resources



Your login username and Slurm account may differ.
Prefer your institution’s managed VS Code service if it provides one. Use its connection and allocation instructions, then follow the project, environment, and notebook steps below in that workspace.
The SSH route below requires your institution to support all three of these:

VS Code and software installation on the login node.
SSH access through the login node to a compute node assigned to you, including any required key setup.
Running the connected VS Code processes inside your Slurm allocation. A matching computer name alone does not establish this; the cluster must support this connection method.

These are cluster settings to confirm before starting. For example, Harvard documents distinct SSH and tunnel routes. If direct SSH is unsupported, use the institution’s managed service or documented tunnel procedure.

Choose storage for your work
Use a project location accessible from both login and compute nodes. Your institution should identify where to keep software environments, research inputs, and results.
Storage names vary, but the distinctions matter:







Storage characteristic
What it means for your work




Persistent shared storage
Files remain available across allocations; check whether it is backed up.


Scratch storage
Intended for working files; it may have an automatic-deletion policy.


Storage local to a compute node
May disappear or become inaccessible when the allocation ends.



Keep the only copy of important inputs and completed results in storage whose retention and backup arrangements you understand. A saved notebook does not contain every separate file its code produces.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
section: 1. Connect VS Code to the login node
text:
1. Connect VS Code to the login node
On your computer, install VS Code. On macOS, move it into Applications; on Windows, run the installer. SSH creates an encrypted connection to another computer; see VS Code’s SSH client instructions if it is not installed.

Choose View → Extensions and install Remote - SSH, published by Microsoft.
Open View → Command Palette, which searches VS Code’s commands, and select Remote-SSH: Add New SSH Host….
Enter the following command with your username and login address, then choose the configuration file in your user folder to save it:

ssh YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST
Replace both capitalized values; @ separates your username from the computer’s address. Use your institution’s connection command if it differs. From the Command Palette, choose Remote-SSH: Connect to Host… and select the saved host.
Complete sign-in, checking any first-connection host fingerprint against your institution’s published information. Select Linux if asked for the remote operating system. The new window’s lower-left indicator should show SSH: and the login host. See VS Code’s connection instructions.
In this window, Explorer, saved edits, and new terminals use the cluster. A local project copy remains separate; Remote-SSH does not synchronize it automatically.
Use this window to prepare the project and request resources.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
section: 2. Create or open your research project
text:
2. Create or open your research project
In the remote VS Code window, choose File → Open Folder and open your approved shared storage location.
For a new project, right-click that folder in Explorer and choose New Folder to create a folder such as memory-project. Open it with File → Open Folder, confirm trust if prompted, then create notebooks, data, and results folders inside it.
If you already have a research project on your computer, transfer its notebooks, required inputs, and environment configuration to this location using the file-transfer instructions below. You can also create and edit notebooks directly on the cluster.
This folder belongs to your research. JAXCMR will be installed into its Python environment.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
section: 3. Install the project’s software on the cluster
text:
3. Install the project’s software on the cluster
Open Terminal → New Terminal in the remote project folder. A terminal accepts commands; enter each command and press Return or Enter. Use pwd to print the current folder and check that it is your project.
Python runs the calculations; uv installs Python and the packages the project needs. Check that Git and uv are available:
git --version
uv --version
Git is used to fetch JAXCMR during installation. Use your institution’s software modules or installation instructions if either command is unavailable.






NoteIf Git or uv is unavailable





Some clusters provide software through environment modules. A command such as module load NAME selects an administrator-installed package and adjusts the current terminal so it can find that software. Replace NAME with your institution’s actual module name and version. This selects existing software; uv installs Python packages for your project. Record any required module commands, since new sessions and jobs may need them again. If Git and uv are already available, no extra module is needed. See the Environment Modules documentation.
If your institution provides uv, use that installation. Otherwise, where user installations are permitted, run:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
The first command downloads and runs uv’s installer. For its default installation location, the second makes uv available in this terminal: $HOME is your cluster home folder, and source applies settings from the named file. If downloads are restricted, use your institution’s supported installation route.




For a new project
Run:
uv init --bare --python 3.12 --vcs none
uv python pin 3.12
uv add "jaxcmr @ git+https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git@main" ipykernel pandas
These commands create the project’s software configuration, select Python 3.12, and install JAXCMR, notebook support, and table-handling tools. The initialization options keep the starting files minimal and leave version-control setup to you. uv downloads Python if needed and permitted by your cluster.
The installed environment is stored in .venv. The configuration files—pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version—record what it needs. The local guide explains these files.


For a project transferred from your computer
If you transferred those configuration files from an existing uv project, run:
uv sync --locked
This creates the cluster’s .venv using the recorded dependencies. It checks that the configuration and lockfile agree rather than silently changing the recorded dependency selection. See uv’s locking and syncing guidance.
Create the environment on the cluster even if you already have one locally. Installed environments contain software specific to the computer where they were created.
Wait for installation to finish successfully before continuing.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
4. Request computing resources
An interactive allocation gives you temporary resources for commands entered in a terminal. Use your institution’s interactive-access command if it provides one. Otherwise, this is a standard Slurm example, run from the login node with memory-project as the current folder:
srun \
  --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT \
  --partition=YOUR_CPU_PARTITION \
  --nodes=1 \
  --ntasks=1 \
  --cpus-per-task=1 \
  --mem=4G \
  --time=00:30:00 \
  --pty bash
Replace the account and partition. Each backslash continues the same command onto the next line.







Part
Meaning




srun
Requests resources and starts a program


--account
Selects the project allocation


--partition
Selects the group of machines


--nodes=1
Uses one compute node


--ntasks=1
Starts one task


--cpus-per-task=1
Allocates one CPU to that task


--mem=4G
Requests 4 GB of memory


--time=00:30:00
Limits the session to thirty minutes after it starts


--pty bash
Opens an interactive command shell on the allocated node



These values suit a small setup check; adapt them to your cluster’s permitted requests and required options. You may wait for resources. See Slurm’s srun documentation.
Once the session starts, run:
hostname
echo "$SLURM_JOB_ID"
Record the computer name and job number: hostname identifies the allocated node; echo prints the job number stored in SLURM_JOB_ID. Keep this terminal and its VS Code window open. They hold the allocation while you connect a second window to the node.
Only this terminal has moved to the compute node. The original VS Code window and its notebook kernels still belong to the login node.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
section: 5. Connect a second window to the compute node
text:
5. Connect a second window to the compute node
For a managed VS Code service, use its allocated workspace and continue to step 6. For the supported SSH route:

Choose File → New Window to open a local VS Code window. Keep the allocation window open.
In the new window, choose Remote-SSH: Open SSH Configuration File… from the Command Palette. Select the local configuration file used in step 1.
Add this entry before any general Host * entry, replacing the capitalized values. COMPUTE_HOST is the allocated node’s SSH address, usually the name printed above. LOGIN_HOST is the login address or configured alias from step 1.

Host jaxcmr-compute
    HostName COMPUTE_HOST
    User YOUR_USERNAME
    ProxyJump YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST
jaxcmr-compute is a convenient connection name. HostName selects the computer, User selects your account, and ProxyJump routes the connection through the login host. Keep any additional authentication settings your institution requires.
Save the file, then use Remote-SSH: Connect to Host… → jaxcmr-compute in this new window. After authentication, its lower-left indicator should show SSH: jaxcmr-compute. Open a new terminal and run hostname; it must match the allocated node, not the login node.
Use File → Open Folder to open the same full memory-project path on shared storage. The files are already there. This second window is now your working window for notebooks.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
6. Work with your own notebooks
A Jupyter notebook is an .ipynb file combining explanations, Python code, and results. Its sections are called cells; code cells run in a Python process called a kernel. VS Code’s Jupyter extension supplies the notebook controls.
In the compute window, open View → Extensions and install Microsoft’s Python and Jupyter extensions for SSH: jaxcmr-compute. Use your institution’s supplied extensions if installation is restricted. Open the shared memory-project folder.
Create a notebook through View → Command Palette → Create: New Jupyter Notebook and save it in notebooks with a filename ending in .ipynb. You can also download a JAXCMR notebook through its documentation page and transfer it to notebooks, or use File → Save As to copy an existing notebook. JAXCMR templates prepare their supplied inputs from the installed package, including on compute nodes without internet access. Transfer your own input files separately and update the notebook’s paths.
Choose Select Kernel → Select Another Kernel → Python Environments and select Python 3.12 from the .venv inside your cluster memory-project folder. If a kernel is already selected, click its name to check or change it.
The notebook controls work as described in Create or download a notebook in the local guide. You can follow that section directly without installing anything on your own computer.
In this window, notebook execution happens on the compute node and saved files belong to the cluster. Selecting an environment in the original login window would run there instead. Keep calculations in the compute window; the login window remains useful for preparing files and managing allocations. See VS Code’s kernel guidance.






NoteOptional: check your installation





Download the first simulation notebook to your computer and transfer it into the cluster project’s notebooks folder. In the compute window, open it, select the project’s .venv, and click Run All. The Colab installation cell skips installation here. The notebook needs no input file; the first calculation may take longer while JAX prepares it.
The final cell should print:
Study order: [1 2 3 4 5]
Simulated recalls: [1 5 2 4 3]
Saved output can be visible before execution, so check that this run finishes without errors. The notebook explains the simulation itself.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
section: 7. Move files between your computer and the cluster
text:
7. Move files between your computer and the cluster
Remote SSH does not automatically synchronize local and cluster copies. You can create notebooks directly on the cluster, but inputs already on your computer must be transferred.
Use your institution’s transfer service if it specifies one. Where ordinary SSH file transfers are supported, scp copies files using your SSH sign-in.
On your own computer, open a local VS Code window, use File → Open Folder to open the folder containing your input file, and choose Terminal → New Terminal. Copy a file to the cluster with:
scp "trials.csv" "YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST:/FULL/PROJECT/PATH/data/"
Replace trials.csv with your filename, the username and host with your sign-in details, and /FULL/PROJECT/PATH with the cluster’s memory-project location. Obtain that full path with Copy Path in the remote Explorer. Create the destination folder first. The first argument is the source; the second is the destination. The colon separates a remote computer’s address from its file path.
To retrieve a results folder, open the desired destination folder locally, open a new terminal there, and run:
scp -r "YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST:/FULL/PROJECT/PATH/results" .
-r copies a folder and its contents; . means the local terminal’s current folder. The same pattern transfers notebooks or other files. Copying can replace matching filenames, and subsequent edits do not synchronize automatically. See the OpenSSH file-copy reference.

Transfer an existing project’s configuration
Use the file-transfer method supported by your institution. Where scp is supported, first create the destination project folder on the cluster.
On your own computer, open the local project folder in VS Code and choose Terminal → New Terminal. Copy its environment configuration with:
scp pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version "YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST:/FULL/PROJECT/PATH/"
Replace the username, login host, and destination with your cluster details. Copy notebooks and inputs using the same method. For the folder arrangement used here:
scp -r notebooks data "YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST:/FULL/PROJECT/PATH/"
Transfer existing results too if the cluster work needs them. Recreate .venv using uv sync --locked in the remote project folder.
After transfer, local and cluster copies remain separate. Update full paths in notebook settings to their cluster locations. Copy completed outputs back using the results-transfer instructions above.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
8. Use inputs and save outputs
Follow Use your own files and Save results and return later in the local guide, using paths copied from the remote Explorer.
Set the notebook’s project path, or its project_root configuration where present, to the cluster’s memory-project folder. A path pointing to your laptop’s Documents folder will not locate the transferred file. After copying an input, check that it appears in the remote Explorer and that the notebook’s input check prints True.
Save tables, figures, and other outputs to shared storage, using separate filenames or folders for runs you want to preserve. You can reopen these files in another allocation or transfer them to your computer. Saving a result file is what makes it available later; leaving a value in Python’s memory does not.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
Finish and return later
Save your notebook and any results you want to retain before ending the allocation. When the allocation’s time limit is reached, its running calculations may be terminated; code that has not yet saved its results cannot be recovered simply by reopening the notebook.
Close the compute connection. In the original allocation terminal, run:
exit
This ends the interactive job and returns that terminal to the login node. Run squeue --jobs=YOUR_JOB_ID, replacing the placeholder with the recorded job number, to check that it has ended. If it remains queued or running, scancel YOUR_JOB_ID cancels that allocation. Closing only the editor window is not a substitute for ending the job.
Your saved files and .venv remain on shared storage according to its retention policy. To return:

Reconnect to the login host and request a new allocation. Load any site-required modules as part of the supported connection procedure.
Update HostName in the existing jaxcmr-compute SSH configuration entry and reconnect the compute window.
Open the same shared project folder and select its .venv.
Run your imports and path settings, then load inputs or saved results.

The environment normally remains available between allocations. If you intentionally transfer updated dependency configuration from another computer, run uv sync --locked before starting notebook kernels. The new session’s Python variables must be recreated by running code. Use Run All when you intend to repeat the whole workflow; otherwise, load saved results and run the subsequent steps you need.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
Continue with JAXCMR
Download Preparing data for JAXCMR, transfer it into the cluster project’s notebooks folder, and open it in an allocated compute window. Then use the templates for analysis and modelling. Select the same .venv environment and choose resources appropriate to the work; the setup allocation above is only for a small check.
Once you have a notebook you can run and inspect, follow Run batches of notebooks unattended on Slurm to submit it without keeping an interactive session open, repeat it with different settings, and manage multiple independent jobs.






NoteOptional: work with the JAXCMR checkout





If you need the complete repository or want to modify JAXCMR itself, follow the local guide’s optional cloning instructions in a cluster terminal, using approved shared storage. The existing template tour uses this route.
Keep that checkout separate from your research project. Open its folder and select its own .venv when working on the library or running repository-dependent examples.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster
text:
If something goes wrong






NoteSSH or VS Code cannot connect





From a local VS Code window, open Terminal → New Terminal and try ssh YOUR_USERNAME@LOGIN_HOST. If ssh is missing, follow the SSH client instructions in step 1. If sign-in fails, check the login address, VPN, and authentication requirements. After a successful terminal test, exit returns to your computer. If SSH works but VS Code does not, inspect View → Output → Remote - SSH.
For the compute connection, confirm that the allocation is still running, HostName names its node, and your institution supports SSH through the login host with your authentication setup. Use its managed service or tunnel procedure where direct SSH is unsupported.









NoteA command is not found





Check which machine the terminal belongs to. On the cluster, confirm that installation completed and load any required software module. For a default uv installation, source "$HOME/.local/bin/env" makes it available in the current terminal.









NoteSlurm rejects the request





Check the account, partition, and permitted resource settings against your allocation. These are cluster access settings, not Python settings.









NoteThe compute node cannot find the project or import JAXCMR





Check pwd, shared storage access, and whether installation finished successfully. Use .venv/bin/python from the intended project folder.









NoteA notebook cannot find an input file





Check that the file was transferred and appears in the remote Explorer. Use Copy Path there to compare its cluster location with the notebook’s settings. A local file path does not refer to the remote copy. Check Path.cwd() inside the notebook if using a relative path.



When asking for help, include the command, complete error message, and whether it ran on your computer, a login node, or a compute node.
crumbs: Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
Use VS Code to write and run Python notebooks, work with your own files, and save results for later. This guide creates your own research project and installs JAXCMR into its Python environment. You can download tutorials and templates to use in that project; cloning the library is optional. No previous experience with Python or VS Code is assumed.
These instructions cover Macs with an Apple chip, such as an M1 or M2, and Windows PCs with a 64-bit Intel or AMD processor. Intel Macs are not supported by this installation route because the required version of JAX does not provide an Intel Mac installer. You will need an internet connection and permission to install software.
If your computer cannot use this route, you can run the code on another computer instead. Follow Remote setup in your browser with Google Colab to prepare a notebook workspace using Google’s computers. If you have access to a research cluster, follow Remote setup with VS Code on a Slurm cluster to prepare it for JAXCMR. Both routes run Python on the remote computer.
On a Mac, choose Apple menu → About This Mac to check: an Apple chip is listed under Chip; an Intel processor is listed under Processor.
The screenshots use dark mode; the same controls are available in light mode. Red boxes mark the controls to look for. The VS Code images show Microsoft examples, so use the JAXCMR filenames and Python version specified in the steps below.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
1. Install VS Code
Visual Studio Code, usually called VS Code, is the application you will use to open project files and work with notebooks.
A Jupyter notebook is a file ending in .ipynb that combines explanations, Python code, and results. Its sections are called cells. Text cells explain the work; code cells contain instructions for Python to execute. The Jupyter extension below gives VS Code its notebook controls.
Download the version for your computer:

Mac: choose the Apple Silicon download. Open the downloaded ZIP file if needed, then move Visual Studio Code to your Applications folder.
Windows: choose the x64 User Installer, open it, and follow the installation steps.

Open VS Code. You will also need two extensions: additions that let VS Code work with Python and the example files used in this guide.

Choose View → Extensions.
Search for Python. Select the extension published by Microsoft and click Install.
Search for Jupyter. Select the extension published by Microsoft and click Install.







Figure 1: Choose Python, published by Microsoft (shown after installation). Repeat the search for Jupyter.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
2. Install Git
The installation command below uses Git to fetch JAXCMR from GitHub, the website where its source is stored. You do not need a GitHub account or a separate checkout of JAXCMR’s repository.
Some of the steps below use a terminal: a panel where you give your computer instructions by typing commands. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal to open it. To run a command, copy it into the terminal and press Return on Mac or Enter on Windows. Do not copy the surrounding box or add any extra characters.






Figure 2: Type commands at the prompt in the Terminal panel. This example shows Windows; the prompt looks different on a Mac.




MacWindows


In the VS Code terminal, run:
xcode-select --install
Follow the prompts to install Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include Git. If you see a message saying the tools are already installed, continue to the next step.


Download the x64 installer from Git for Windows and run it.
Use the default installation options. In particular, keep Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software when asked how Git should be used.



Finish the installation before continuing.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
3. Install uv
Python runs the calculations, and JAXCMR is a package of Python tools for memory research. uv installs Python and the packages this project needs, keeping them together in an environment. This lets notebooks in the project use the same installed software. You do not need to install Python separately.
In VS Code, open Terminal → New Terminal if the terminal is not already open. Run the command for your computer:

MacWindows


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh


Use a PowerShell terminal. If the terminal has a different name, use the arrow beside the + button in the terminal panel and choose PowerShell.






Figure 3: On Windows, use the arrow beside + to choose PowerShell.



powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"



These are the commands from uv’s installation instructions.
When installation finishes, quit VS Code completely and reopen it so it can find Git and uv. On Mac, use Code → Quit Visual Studio Code; on Windows, close all VS Code windows.
Open Terminal → New Terminal and run these commands one at a time:
git --version
uv --version
Each should print its name and a version number, such as git version … and uv …. If either command is not found or not recognized, see If something goes wrong before continuing.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
4. Create your project folder
A project folder keeps the notebooks, inputs, results, and software settings for one piece of research together.
Using Finder or Windows File Explorer, create a folder somewhere convenient, such as Documents. Give it a meaningful name; this guide uses memory-project.
In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and open that folder. If prompted, confirm that you trust the folder you created.
Choose View → Explorer to see the folder in the left-hand panel. Right-click its name and choose New Folder to create each of these three folders:
memory-project/
├── notebooks/
├── data/
└── results/
Keep your notebooks in notebooks, input files in data, and saved outputs in results. These names are suggestions; you can use another arrangement or keep large datasets elsewhere.

title: Local setup with VS Code
section: 5. Install Python and JAXCMR for this project
text:
5. Install Python and JAXCMR for this project
Choose Terminal → New Terminal. The terminal should open inside memory-project.
If you already have a uv-managed research project, open that folder and run only the uv add command below; keep its existing project configuration. For a new project, run all three commands one at a time:
uv init --bare --python 3.12 --vcs none
uv python pin 3.12
uv add "jaxcmr @ git+https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git@main" ipykernel pandas
The first command creates the project’s software configuration. --bare keeps the starting files minimal, and --vcs none leaves version-control setup to you. The second records Python 3.12 as the version to use. See uv’s project commands.
The last command installs:

JAXCMR, from GitHub’s main branch.
ipykernel, which lets VS Code run notebook cells using this environment.
pandas, which provides the table-reading and writing tools used later in this guide.

uv downloads Python if needed and installs the packages in a .venv folder inside your project. Wait for installation to finish successfully before continuing. uv’s VS Code instructions explain the notebook connection.
After installation, your folder also contains:







File or folder
Purpose




pyproject.toml
Records the packages your project uses.


uv.lock
Records the resolved package versions and JAXCMR revision.


.python-version
Records the Python version to use.


.venv
Contains the installed software for this computer.



Keep the three configuration files with your research project. They let uv recreate its environment on another computer. See uv’s project structure.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
6. Create or download a notebook
With memory-project open in VS Code, choose how to begin:

Create your own notebook: open View → Command Palette, which searches VS Code’s commands, run Create: New Jupyter Notebook, and use File → Save As to save it in notebooks with a filename ending in .ipynb.
Use a JAXCMR tutorial or template: open its documentation page and choose Download notebook. Move the downloaded file into notebooks, then open it in VS Code.
Continue existing work: open its notebook from Explorer.

Choose Select Kernel → Select Another Kernel → Python Environments and select the Python 3.12 .venv inside your memory-project folder. If Python Environments is already shown, choose it directly. A kernel is the running Python process; the selected environment supplies its installed packages. Use that environment for each notebook belonging to this project. If a kernel is already selected, click its name to check or change it.






Figure 4: Click Select Kernel at the upper right to choose the Python environment for this notebook.




Downloading a notebook and its inputs
A notebook download contains its code, explanations, and saved cell outputs. Separate input files must also be available.
The data-preparation tutorial creates its small teaching dataset in code. The templates copy their supplied inputs from the installed package; the templates page describes these files and provides optional individual downloads.
The templates prepare their supplied example inputs from the installed package, on your computer as well as in Colab. Supply your own files separately and update the input paths when adapting a template.
When a notebook has a project_root setting, set it to the full path of memory-project. In Explorer, right-click that folder and choose Copy Path. For example:
project_root = r"PASTE_PROJECT_PATH_HERE"
Replace the text between the quotation marks. This makes the notebook’s relative input and output paths refer to your project folder, even though the notebook itself is saved inside notebooks.
Check its input and output settings before running. The next section explains file paths in more detail.


Work with cells
Use + Code to add Python instructions and + Markdown to add explanatory text. Click inside a code cell to edit it. Run it with the triangle beside the cell or Shift+Enter; its output appears underneath. Run All executes the notebook from top to bottom. See VS Code’s notebook controls.
Cells use values created by earlier executions. Changing a value in an earlier cell requires running that cell again, followed by the cells that depend on it. Editing code alone does not update the results.
Arrange your notebook so it can run in order: imports and settings, loading files, calculations, then saving results. Stop and resolve an error before running cells that depend on the failed step.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
7. Use your own files
Copy your input files into the project’s data folder using Finder or Windows File Explorer, or leave them in an existing location and use their full paths.
A path identifies a file or folder. A full path starts from your computer’s filesystem root or drive. A relative path, such as data/trials.csv, is interpreted from Python’s current working folder. That folder can differ from the terminal’s; inspect it inside the notebook with:
from pathlib import Path

print(Path.cwd())
For a straightforward starting arrangement, use a full project path. In VS Code’s Explorer, right-click memory-project and choose Copy Path. Paste it between the quotation marks below, replacing PASTE_PROJECT_PATH_HERE:
project = Path(r"PASTE_PROJECT_PATH_HERE")
input_path = project / "data" / "trials.csv"
output_dir = project / "results"
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

print("Input file exists:", input_path.is_file())
print("Save results in:", output_dir)
Keep the r before the quotation mark; it allows Windows paths containing backslashes. Replace trials.csv with your filename. / joins path components, and mkdir creates the output folder if needed. If the input check prints False, compare the path with the file’s actual location and spelling. These operations use Python’s path tools.
For a CSV table, load and inspect it with:
import pandas as pd

table = pd.read_csv(input_path)
table.head()
pandas is installed with this workspace. The import makes its tools available as pd; table holds the loaded data in Python’s memory, and head() displays its first few rows. Other file formats need a suitable reader. See pandas’ CSV reader.
When adapting a JAXCMR template, edit its existing configuration cell: set project_root to your project’s full path and adjust its input and output settings. Check additional locations such as simulation_dir or figure_dir where present. Moving a notebook does not automatically change the files it reads or writes.
Preparing data for JAXCMR explains the data format needed for modelling.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
8. Save results and return later
File → Save preserves the notebook’s code, explanations, and displayed outputs. To use a result in another notebook or application, write it as a separate file.
For example, save the table loaded above as a CSV:
saved_path = output_dir / "trials-copy.csv"
table.to_csv(saved_path, index=False)
print(saved_path)
index=False leaves out pandas’ extra row-number column. After an analysis, use this pattern with its result table and a meaningful filename. Choose distinct filenames or folders for results you want to retain separately; saving to an existing filename can replace it. See pandas’ CSV writer.
Find the saved file in Explorer. A figure needs its own save operation; JAXCMR templates save files according to their output settings.
Closing VS Code leaves your saved files and installed environment on disk. A new or restarted kernel begins without the previous session’s Python variables. Restart Kernel clears that running state without removing installed packages. Results already visible in a notebook may be saved output from an earlier session.
When returning:

Use File → Open Folder to open memory-project, then open your notebook.
Select the project’s .venv.
Run the imports and path settings.
Load your inputs or previously saved results, then run the calculations you need.







Figure 5: You can also find File: Open Folder… in the Command Palette to reopen your memory-project folder.



For example, after defining project and importing pandas, a later notebook can read the saved table:
saved_table = pd.read_csv(project / "results" / "trials-copy.csv")
Saved files let separate notebooks share results. Using the same environment gives them access to the same packages; it does not automatically share their variables. You normally do not repeat installation for each notebook.
Use Run All when you intend to repeat the whole workflow. To continue from saved results, load those files and run the subsequent steps.

Add software or move to another computer
You normally install packages once per project. If another notebook needs an additional package, add it from a terminal in this folder using uv add PACKAGE_NAME, replacing the placeholder with that package’s name. This records the dependency as well as installing it. See Managing project dependencies.
On another computer, copy pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version along with the notebooks and data you need. Install uv there (and Git if the project installs from GitHub), open the copied project folder, and recreate the environment with:
uv sync --locked
Recreate .venv on the destination computer rather than copying it. Keep backups of your notebooks, inputs, results, and configuration files.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
Continue with JAXCMR
Download Preparing data for JAXCMR into notebooks, then use the templates for analysis and modelling. Apply the same notebook, input-path, and output-path choices when moving to your own work. The existing template tour uses the optional repository checkout below.






NoteOptional: check your installation





Download the first simulation notebook, move it into notebooks, and open it in VS Code. Select the Python 3.12 .venv inside your memory-project folder. This supplied notebook needs no input file.
Click Run All at the top of the notebook. This runs its code cells in order, so later cells can use what earlier cells have prepared. The first cell is for Colab and skips installation on your computer.






Figure 6: Run All executes the notebook from the beginning. Each code cell displays its results underneath it.



You may already see saved results when you open the file; they do not mean its code has run in your current session. Run All computes them again. Wait for execution to finish; the first run may take longer while JAX prepares the calculation. If a cell reports an error, resolve it before continuing.
The last code cell prints:
Study order: [1 2 3 4 5]
Simulated recalls: [1 5 2 4 3]
Reaching this output confirms that the selected Python environment can load JAXCMR and execute a model. The notebook’s Read the output section explains the simulation.
Completing this check verifies installation; use the earlier sections to work with your own notebooks and files.









NoteOptional: get the complete JAXCMR repository





JAXCMR’s repository contains its source code, examples, and documentation. Cloning downloads a checkout of that collection. Use this route if you want to work on the library itself or obtain the complete examples. The existing template tour, which coordinates several notebooks and supplied datasets, currently uses this route.
Keep the checkout in a separate folder beside your research project. In VS Code, open the parent folder, such as Documents, choose Terminal → New Terminal, and run:
git clone https://github.com/githubpsyche/jaxcmr.git
cd jaxcmr
uv sync --locked
The first command downloads the repository into a new jaxcmr folder, cd moves the terminal into it, and uv sync --locked installs its recorded software environment.
Open the resulting jaxcmr folder with File → Open Folder, confirm trust if prompted, and select its .venv when working through repository examples or modifying the library. Return to your research folder and its environment for your own project.

title: Local setup with VS Code
text:
If something goes wrong

Git or uv is not found
Quit VS Code completely, reopen it, and open a new terminal. Try git --version and uv --version again. If a command is still missing, check that its installation finished successfully.


uv cannot find pyproject.toml
The terminal is probably in the wrong folder. Use File → Open Folder to open your research folder containing pyproject.toml, then open a new terminal and retry the command. For a new folder without that file, complete step 5 first.


.venv is not listed as a kernel
Check that the uv add installation in step 5, or uv sync --locked for a copied project, finished successfully. Quit and reopen VS Code, reopen the notebook, and try the kernel picker again.


The notebook says No module named jaxcmr
Check that installation finished in your research project folder and that the notebook’s selected kernel uses the .venv inside that folder. Select that environment, then rerun the cell that imports JAXCMR.


A name is not defined
Run the earlier cell that defines that name, including imports and path settings. Variables from a previous kernel session or a different notebook are not automatically available.


A file is not found
Compare the filename and location with Copy Path in Explorer. Check Path.cwd() if using a relative path. Moving or copying a notebook does not move its input files or update its path settings.


JAX reports a DLL error on Windows
JAX may also need Microsoft’s Visual C++ Redistributable for x64. Install it, restart VS Code, and try running the notebook again. This requirement is described in JAX’s installation instructions.
If you ask for help, include the step you reached and the complete error message.






NoteScreenshot sources





VS Code screenshots: Microsoft, CC BY 3.0 US. Sources: extensions, terminal, Command Palette, and notebooks. Red highlights have been added where needed; the source images are unchanged.

title: JAXCMR documentation
text:
Computational models of memory describe how people learn and retrieve information. Implementing these models and comparing their predictions with experimental data can require substantial programming.
jaxcmr is a Python package for computational memory research. It leverages a compositional design and JAX’s support for just-in-time compilation, vectorization, and automatic differentiation to streamline data analysis and model development so researchers can explore more ideas in less time.
If you use jaxcmr, please cite the paper [citation to be added].
See the code repository for version release notes.
