title: Fitting Procedures
text:
What the template adds
A FitResult is not a complete experiment specification. The fitting template saves additional fields for the observation source and selection, model factory, component creators, loss, package version, numerical precision, input paths and run settings. It also saves the objective recalculated from the returned parameters. These are project conventions added around the fitter’s result.
Data Simulation consumes the returned parameter values with an explicit assignment to participant IDs. Applying pooled values to participants requires that assignment; the -1 label is not a participant in the observation dataset. Model Evaluation uses the objective and saved settings to establish which comparisons are appropriate.
The fitting template supplies the complete configuration, optimization, saving, objective recalculation and subsequent simulation. This guide explains the interfaces that procedure connects.
The supplied CMR fit estimates nine continuous parameters with learning before context updating and repeated recalls disabled. Preparation compared seeds 0 and 1, each with three restarts; search_comparison retains both results and the selected seed. These are preparation metadata, not required FitResult fields. Recorded paths and versions describe the run but cannot detect edits in place. Refit after changing observations or model code; matching parameter names do not establish that a model has the same meaning.

title: Fitting Procedures
section: Selecting an optimizer in the template

title: Fitting Procedures
section: Reusing fits and aligning participant parameters
text:
Reusing fits and aligning participant parameters
Saved workflows may add model/input identities and a fit_configuration to a FitResult. These are optional workflow metadata, rather than additional required fields of the core result type. The public record operations work on in-memory mappings and can be used from scripts as well as notebooks.
from jaxcmr.fitting import validate_fit_compatibility, combine_participant_parameters

validate_fit_compatibility(saved_fit, requested_configuration)
parameters = combine_participant_parameters([fit_a["fits"], fit_b["fits"]])
requested_configuration contains the requested fixed/free parameters, search_settings, selected_trial_indices, model_factory, components and loss_function. Input paths and feature settings are compared when recorded; missing descriptions in older records cannot identify their inputs. Display-only optimizer options and obsolete digest fields are ignored. Recalculate the objective before reusing a fit, and refit after changing data or code in place.
combine_participant_parameters combines compatible participant parameter columns, sorts all columns by subject ID, and preserves boolean values. It rejects duplicate IDs, pooled rows (subject=-1), inconsistent keys and misaligned columns. First establish model and observation compatibility; the function does not do that for you. Its return value contains parameter rows only, not merged optimizer diagnostics or a complete FitResult. Both inputs remain unchanged.

title: Fitting Procedures
section: Assigning a fit to the participants being simulated
text:
Assigning a fit to the participants being simulated
After checking that a saved fit is suitable for the requested model and data, parameters_for_subjects prepares parameter arrays for dataset simulation:
from jaxcmr.fitting import parameters_for_subjects

subject_parameters = parameters_for_subjects(saved_fit, [12, 5])
# Pass subject_parameters to simulate_h5_from_h5 with your model and trial mask.
Every returned column is a new JAX array aligned to participants 12 and 5, in that order. Both fit-record utilities normalize integer-valued participant IDs such as 3.0; booleans and fractional IDs are rejected. Participant fits are matched by identity, rather than row position. A pooled fit broadcasts its single subject=-1 row to the requested participants. Older records without a pooled field are recognized by that sentinel. Boolean parameter types are restored using optional fit_configuration.parameters.fixed metadata, falling back to fixed. These metadata fields are not additional required fields of FitResult.
Missing participants, duplicate IDs, inconsistent column lengths and conflicting pooled declarations raise errors. The original record is unchanged. Unlike combine_participant_parameters, which assembles separate participant fits, this operation assigns one record’s values to a requested participant sequence. It does not load files, construct a model, or validate whether the fitted model and observations are scientifically compatible. Keep those checks and the decision to use pooled or participant fits in your procedure.

title: Memory Search Models
text: A memory-search model exposes study and retrieval operations that losses and simulators can use. The model determines how its internal state changes and how that state supports possible responses. MemorySearch describes the shared interface, while a model factory connects an experiment and its parameters to fresh model instances.

title: Memory Search Models
text:
The model interface
A compatible model supplies the attributes and methods in MemorySearch. The selected declaration below shows the event lifecycle and probabilities; the complete protocol also exposes item eligibility and retrieval activations.
Selected declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class MemorySearch(Protocol):
    item_count: int
    is_active: Bool[Array, ""]
    studied: Bool[Array, " item_count"]
    recall_total: Integer[Array, ""]
    study_index: Integer[Array, ""]

    def experience(self, choice: Int_) -> "MemorySearch": ...

    def start_retrieving(self) -> "MemorySearch": ...

    def retrieve(self, choice: Int_) -> "MemorySearch": ...

    def outcome_probability(self, choice: Int_) -> Float[Array, ""]: ...

    def outcome_probabilities(self) -> Float[Array, " recall_outcomes"]: ...







Operation
Meaning




experience(choice)
Process a one-based within-list item code; zero is ignored.


start_retrieving()
Make the transition from study to retrieval.


outcome_probabilities()
Return the next-response distribution, with stop at index zero and item codes at their positive indices.


retrieve(choice)
Update after a supplied item or stop event; zero stops retrieval.



State-changing methods return the updated model. Callers retain that return value rather than assuming the original object was mutated. Parameters such as context drift and learning rates configure the calculations; the changing state includes context, learned associations and recall eligibility.
A likelihood supplies the recorded events, obtains their probabilities and advances the model. A simulator samples events and advances the model. Both can consume a compatible model without depending on its particular equations. JAX transformations also require the implementation’s state and operations to work with JAX.

title: Memory Search Models
text:
Factories connect models to experiments
Declaration from jaxcmr.typing:
class MemorySearchModelFactory(Protocol):
    def __init__(
        self,
        dataset: RecallDataset,
        features: Float[Array, " word_pool_items features_count"] | None,
    ) -> None: ...

    def create_model(
        self, parameters: Mapping[str, Float_]
    ) -> MemorySearch: ...

    def create_trial_model(
        self, trial_index: Integer[Array, ""], parameters: Mapping[str, Float_]
    ) -> MemorySearch: ...
A factory class is passed as model_factory_cls to a loss or simulator. Its constructor receives the dataset and optional vocabulary features. The resulting factory instance creates fresh models from parameters. create_trial_model() additionally receives a dataset row index, allowing trial-specific stimulus features or conditions to affect construction.
For ordinary CMR, jaxcmr.models.cmr.make_factory() binds component creators and returns this factory class. Its models use the dataset’s maximum list length; the ordinary factory does not use trial-specific features. Other factories can require fields such as pres_itemids or valence.
This is the model entry point for existing workflows: supply a compatible factory through model_factory_cls. Matching method names alone does not establish suitable event coding or scientific assumptions.
Semantic factories check that pres_itemids aligns with study positions and that positive integer IDs are covered by the supplied vocabulary features or similarity matrix. A similarity matrix must be square. These checks occur once during factory preparation, outside the compiled model calculations; they do not impose a similarity scale or symmetry requirement.


0 — Locate the project inputs
from pathlib import Path

from jaxcmr.helpers import find_project_root, resolve_project_path

try:
    root_path = Path(find_project_root())
except FileNotFoundError:
    root_path = Path.cwd()




Create a model through a CMR factory
from pathlib import Path
import json
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxcmr.helpers import load_data, generate_trial_mask
from jaxcmr.components import context, linear_memory
from jaxcmr.components.termination import NoStopTermination
from jaxcmr.models.cmr import make_factory

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
data = load_data(resolve_project_path("data/Dupertuys2026.h5", root_path))
record = json.loads(Path(resolve_project_path("data/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo.json", root_path)).read_text())
parameters = {name: values[0] for name, values in record["fits"].items()
              if name != "subject"}
for name in ("allow_repeated_recalls", "learn_after_context_update"):
    parameters[name] = bool(parameters[name])

CMRFactory = make_factory(
    mfc_create_fn=linear_memory.init_mfc,
    mcf_create_fn=linear_memory.init_mcf,
    context_create_fn=context.init,
    termination_policy_create_fn=NoStopTermination,
)

factory = CMRFactory(data, features=None)
mixed = generate_trial_mask(data, "data['list_type'] == 1")
trial_index = int(jnp.flatnonzero(mixed)[0])
initial = factory.create_trial_model(trial_index, parameters)
print("Model:", type(initial).__name__)
print("Item capacity:", initial.item_count)
print("Initial study count:", int(initial.study_index))


Model: CMR
Item capacity: 12
Initial study count: 0


The factory configuration above selects CMR with linear associative memories, temporal context and a no-stop policy. Parameter values come from the supplied demonstration fit, but a model can equally use hand-chosen values. Model Components explains the creator functions.

title: Memory Search Models
section: Following one event through the interface
text:
Following one event through the interface
Study events already contain within-list item codes. Recorded recalls contain study positions, so the caller translates the first response through pres_itemnos before passing it to retrieve().


Inspect state and probabilities across one retrieval
studied = initial
for item in data["pres_itemnos"][trial_index]:
    studied = studied.experience(item)
ready = studied.start_retrieving()
position = int(data["recalls"][trial_index, 0])
first_item = int(data["pres_itemnos"][trial_index, position - 1])
after = ready.retrieve(first_item)

print("Study counts, original and updated:",
      int(initial.study_index), int(studied.study_index))
print("Recall count after retrieval:", int(after.recall_total))
print("Probability of this item before retrieval:",
      float(ready.outcome_probability(first_item)))
print("Probability of this item after retrieval:",
      float(after.outcome_probability(first_item)))
print("Next-response vector shape:", after.outcome_probabilities().shape)


Study counts, original and updated: 0 12
Recall count after retrieval: 1
Probability of this item before retrieval: 0.13703638099013163
Probability of this item after retrieval: 0.0
Next-response vector shape: (13,)


The original model remains unstudied. The updated model has processed a complete list and one response. With repeated recalls disabled, the recalled item is no longer eligible; the remaining response distribution reflects the changed state. A no-stop policy contributes no voluntary stopping mechanism while candidates remain available.
The fitting template uses this factory configuration in a complete procedure. This page’s event illustration establishes the interface used by that procedure, not a test of CMR theory.

title: Templates
text:
A template is a maintained notebook for a complete procedure: selecting observations, performing a calculation and saving interpretable results. Its parameters cell specifies one run. Changing those settings lets you reuse the procedure for another selection, model or experiment, or prepare many independent jobs without maintaining a separate procedure for each one.
These fourteen templates cover behavioral analysis, fitting, simulation, parameter exploration and pooled model comparison. Their defaults use the war-photo-recall experiment as a shared worked example. The saved figures and tables show that example; they are replaced when you execute a new run. Choose a task below, then download its notebook. Its setup prepares the supplied inputs from the installed package; provide your own files when adapting it to your research.
The procedures connect through saved products:
The shared example compares ordinary CMR, source-only eCMR and broader eCMR. To inspect completed runs, use the supplied fits and responses. To change the scientific specification, configure the fitting or intervention procedure and pass its saved outputs to the analyses. The local instructions explain preparation and execution.

title: Templates
text:
The experiment
In this experiment, Dupertuys and colleagues asked whether emotion changes both which pictures people remember and the order in which they remember them. Participants studied photographs relating to the war in Ukraine, then recalled them from memory. The final sample comprised 123 English-speaking adults selected for their reported concern about the war.
Each participant completed four rounds, each with two phases:

Study the photographs. A list contained twelve target photographs, plus an extra “buffer” photograph at each end. Each image appeared for six seconds, followed by a three-second blank screen.
Recall the photographs. Immediately after the list, participants typed short descriptions of as many photographs as they could remember, in any order. They then continued to the next study-and-recall round.

Researchers later scored the typed responses by matching descriptions to photograph identities, retaining the order in which the pictures were recalled.
The lists differed in their emotional composition. Emotional photographs were rated as more negative and more arousing; neutral photographs were the less negative, less arousing comparison images from the same war-related set. Every participant encountered all three conditions:








List condition
Target photographs in each list
Lists per participant




Mixed
6 emotional and 6 neutral
2


Pure emotional
12 emotional
1


Pure neutral
12 neutral
1



List order was counterbalanced across participants, and target-picture order was randomized within each list. Targets were not repeated across a participant’s four lists.
Mixed lists let us compare emotional and neutral recall within the same list. Pure lists let us ask how that difference changes when the two types of picture are studied separately. Recording recall order also lets us examine memory search: for example, whether one recalled picture tends to be followed by a picture studied nearby in time, or by a picture with similar meaning.

title: Templates
section: The data used in the templates
text:
The data used in the templates
The supplied file contains 492 list records: 246 mixed, 123 pure-emotional and 123 pure-neutral. Photographs are represented by item identifiers, and recall responses by scored sequences. Buffer photographs are excluded, so the study positions used in these templates refer to the twelve target photographs. One pure-emotional record contains eleven valid target items and a padded slot; the fixed-length analyses identify and exclude that record.







Field
Meaning in these procedures




subject
Participant identifier, retained when simulating.


list_type
Whole-list condition: 1 = mixed, 2 = pure emotional, 3 = pure neutral.


pres_itemnos
Studied item codes within a trial; zero is a padded slot.


pres_itemids
Global picture identifiers used to align the distance matrix and categories.


recalls
One-based study positions of recalled items; zero is an unused response slot.


valence
Category at each study position: −1 = emotional, 0 = neutral. Check valid study items before counting categories.



Study positions and item identities are different: a recall code of 3 points to the third study slot, whose global picture identifier is found in pres_itemids. The supplied distance matrix is indexed by global identifier minus one. Its missing entries are outside the within-list comparisons used here; every within-list pair required by the semantic examples has a finite distance.
Selections are made in notebook cells and leave the source file unchanged:

Fitting and pooled model comparison: all 492 lists and all conditions.
SPC, PNR, stopping and temporal organization: the 491 complete twelve-item lists. Each notebook explicitly reports the one excluded padded list.
Semantic organization: the 246 mixed lists and the supplied distance matrix.
Category recall rate: all conditions, with valid-item denominators.
Category SPC and category-CRP: mixed lists by default.

Plots summarize each participant’s selected lists before averaging across participants. Error bars describe bootstrap intervals for those participant summaries. Some bins have no variation or no defined values, so the current plotters can report that a bootstrap interval is undefined; this does not turn an unavailable category or transition into a zero-valued observation.

Download the shared inputs

The observations and distance matrix describe the war-photo-recall experiment. The example-fit methods identify the models, searches and assumptions behind the three supplied fit records. Response examples were generated with ten repetitions per selected list and seed 1. Their JSON files record the parameters, selections and simulation settings. These are saved inputs to analysis: analysis notebooks do not fit or simulate when an input is missing.
Each template page has Download notebook and Open in Colab links beside its contents list. Colab opens the latest notebook on GitHub’s main branch. In a local preview, the download includes local edits while Colab still opens the last pushed version. Code is expanded by default. Collapse individual labeled blocks or use the Code menu to hide or show all code. Figures and tables remain visible.

title: Templates
text:
Run in Colab
Use Open in Colab on a template page, then save your own copy before editing. The Colab setup guide explains running cells, using your own files and keeping outputs between sessions.
Keep the template’s short installation cell and input-preparation call. The cell installs JAXCMR from GitHub’s main branch; input preparation copies selected examples from that installation. Update the installation when you need newer library code or examples. Custom input files remain yours to provide. Colab labels the first raw cell “Unsupported Cell Type”; it contains website metadata and is skipped during execution.

title: Templates
section: From a template to a run
text:
From a template to a run
Save downloaded notebooks in your working folder, beside data/. Open the folder in your notebook editor, select its Python environment, edit the parameters cell and run the notebook from top to bottom. Relative paths follow the project-directory rules below. Give independent runs distinct output folders or run names so their results do not overwrite one another.

Paths and working directories
The project_root parameter selects the base for all relative input and output paths:







Setting or execution context
Base directory




An explicit project_root
That directory; a relative value uses the kernel’s starting directory.


Local checkout, project_root=None
The enclosing Git root, found by the existing find_project_root() helper.


Standalone folder, project_root=None
The kernel’s working directory.


Colab, project_root=None
The runtime’s working directory.



The notebook reports the chosen directory. Running from templates/ or a nested prepared-job directory inside a checkout uses the same project inputs and outputs. When the kernel starts outside the project, supply project_root explicitly. The root belongs to your research project; it is not the installed JAXCMR package directory.
Absolute paths remain absolute, and ~ expands to your home directory. On Windows, "C:/Users/Alex/my-study" or r"C:\Users\Alex\my-study" works; avoid a partially specified drive path such as "C:my-study". UNC paths are supported on Windows. Relative defaults such as "data/Dupertuys2026.h5" work on both platforms. An absolute path from another computer must be updated there.
The input helper copies recognized relative example names into this same base on every platform. Custom files remain your responsibility; selecting an absolute custom path does not download an example over it. Path resolution happens after parameter injection and does not change the process’s working directory.


Saved products and regeneration
Copy the fit_paths printed by fitting into simulation, then supply the printed simulation_paths to model comparison or their values as analysis data_paths. The defaults continue to use the supplied examples until you replace them. For example, a one-model simulation job can use:
fit_paths = {"CMR": "results/fits/Dupertuys2026_CMR_demo_best_of_3.json"}
output_dir supplies default locations, but explicit directory settings take precedence:







Procedure
Directory precedence




Fitting
target_directory or output_dir supplies the product root; explicit fit_dir, simulation_dir and figure_dir override their defaults.


Simulation
Explicit simulation_dir and figure_dir override output_dir. The example sets simulation_dir="results/simulations".


Parameter shifting, model comparison and analyses
Explicit figure_dir overrides its default; summary tables use output_dir.



Give independent jobs distinct names or directories for every product they write. redo_fits=False reuses a matching existing fit; a missing fit is still computed and an incompatible record is reported. redo_sims=False permits matching response reuse; when predictions are requested, missing or stale responses are regenerated. Fitting is fit-only when both redo_sims and redo_figures are false. figure_str="" disables figure saving, but does not disable summary CSVs.
Reuse checks compare saved settings and, for fits, independently recalculate the objective. They do not detect edits to data or code in place. After such changes, set redo_fits=True and/or redo_sims=True for the affected calculations, or use a new output location. A matching path is not proof of matching file contents.
Settings are ordinary values: paths, numbers, lists, dictionaries and import names. Imports, trial masks and model construction happen afterward, using the effective values. The fitting template can select a model and its components, objective, fitted parameters, participant subset and displayed analyses. Analysis templates expose their trial selections and measure-specific settings. Their inputs are saved response files; preparing or running an analysis does not generate missing simulations.
Ordinary imports occupy their own cell after the optional Colab bootstrap. Derived paths, loading and calculations follow the injected parameters. figure_str="" displays figures without saving them; a nonempty name saves under figure_dir. The defaults provide explicit names for the worked examples. Subject-level CSV summaries use output_dir.
The analysis controls include repeated-item capacity (size), stopping mode, condition queries, category fields and labels, and plot limits. Category recall also accepts configured paired contrasts and contrasts of contrasts. Select these for the question being asked; the defaults leave the optional tests empty.
You can also supply settings externally. Quarto and Papermill use the same tagged cell. An override replaces a whole top-level value: to change one model, supply the complete model_configs dictionary for that work unit. Use fit_alg_path and fit_hyperparams to select and configure the optimizer. Analysis templates use data_paths and data_labels for a collection; an explicit data_path retains single-dataset use. Their condition queries are applied to each input.


Execute a report with Quarto
With Quarto installed, you can execute a notebook with overrides and render its results to HTML. Python parameter injection uses Papermill, which the repository’s default uv sync already installs. For this example, run from the repository root and select the environment for Quarto using the command for your shell:

macOS / LinuxWindows PowerShell


export QUARTO_PYTHON="$(uv run python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')"


$env:QUARTO_PYTHON = (uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)")



Then run the same command on either platform:
quarto render templates/pnr.ipynb --execute -P query_recall_position:2 -P output_dir:results/pnr-third --output pnr-third.html
Quarto normally executes from the notebook’s directory; the template’s root lookup handles that. An injected project_root also works for notebooks prepared outside the project. The website build does not execute notebooks.
Output positions are zero-based, so 2 means the third response. Use --execute-params settings.yml for dictionaries or longer selections. The explicit --execute runs the notebook; rendering an .ipynb without it normally displays its stored results. The website displays saved example outputs.


Prepare independent jobs with Papermill
For a cluster batch, it can be useful to inspect the complete set of jobs before executing any of them. Papermill’s prepare_only=True creates a configured notebook for each job. From the repository root, the following Python cell prepares two fitting runs that differ only in optimization seed and output folder:


Prepare two fitting jobs without running them
from pathlib import Path
from copy import deepcopy
import nbformat
import papermill as pm

source = nbformat.read("templates/fitting.ipynb", as_version=4)
defaults = {}
parameter_cell = next(cell for cell in source.cells
                      if "parameters" in cell.metadata.get("tags", []))
# Evaluate only the parameter assignments, not the fitting procedure.
exec(parameter_cell.source, defaults)

jobs = Path("analyses/rendered")
jobs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for seed in [0, 1]:
    configs = deepcopy(defaults["model_configs"])
    for config in configs.values():
        config["seed"] = seed
    path = jobs / f"fitting_seed_{seed}.ipynb"
    prepared = pm.execute_notebook(
        "templates/fitting.ipynb", str(path),
        parameters={"model_configs": configs, "output_dir": f"results/fitting-seed-{seed}"},
        prepare_only=True,
    )
    # Stored example results are not results from this new job.
    for cell in prepared.cells:
        if cell.cell_type == "code":
            cell.outputs = []
            cell.execution_count = None
    nbformat.write(prepared, path)


To prepare one model per job, pass a one-entry model_configs dictionary. Preserve the project’s chosen job boundaries: a model collection does not require running every model in each scheduled job. Inspect the injected settings in each notebook. Execute one from the working folder with:
uv run papermill analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb analyses/rendered/fitting_seed_0.ipynb --cwd .
The same prepared notebooks can be transferred with their inputs and run as separate Slurm jobs, using the project folder as the working directory. This keeps the prepared paths portable: set --cwd to the destination project folder, or inject its project_root when executing. Do not inject a local machine’s absolute root into jobs intended for a different machine. This matches the remote-cluster workflow: maintain a procedure, prepare concrete work units, then schedule their execution. Preparing jobs does not fit a model; rendering HTML is a separate presentation step.
For participant jobs, the fitting template uses pooled=False and subject_indices=[i], where i indexes the sorted participant IDs. Simulation and parameter exploration can instead vary seeds or parameter values. Choose the work unit around the scientific question and keep its inputs and outputs explicit. A fit-only job sets both redo_sims and redo_figures to False; later simulation can use its saved result.

title: Templates

Modeling procedures
The example collection estimates nine continuous CMR parameters and ten for each eCMR variant, using the same observations and termination-excluded likelihood. The two eCMR specifications differ in whether emotional modulation also affects temporal association learning. The default simulator conditions on observed recall counts. Recall length, stopping distributions and pure-list category totals therefore are imposed; mixed-list category allocation and recall organization can vary.
Simulation and parameter shifting start from the supplied fits without optimization. The latter includes encoding-drift sweeps and a separate controlled temporal-emotional-modulation switch. Model comparison consumes the saved fits and responses. Its results describe pooled solutions, not independent participant estimates. Each procedure remains configurable for other inputs, models and scientific questions.

title: Serial position curves by category

Use this procedure to ask how category differences in recall vary across study positions. It reads response files with per-position category codes and saves category-specific serial position curves.
Each category has its own presentation opportunities at each position. An absent category-position combination is undefined, rather than evidence that recall probability is zero.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Serial position curves by category
text:
Interpret category-specific recall by position
For each participant, the numerator counts recalls of category items at a position and the denominator counts presentations of that category at that position. Padded positions are removed before calculation. The figure summarizes participant curves with bootstrap confidence intervals.
A missing category at a position produces an undefined value, which can change the participants contributing there. With repeated recalls, this existing calculation counts recall events; the category recall-rate template instead counts whether each position was recalled. Keep that distinction in mind for data allowing repetitions.

title: Lag-conditional response probability
text:
Use lag-conditional response probability (lag-CRP) to ask whether successive recalls favor nearby study positions, and whether forward and backward transitions differ. The procedure reads response files, compares chosen transitions with available opportunities, and saves a curve.
Positive lag means moving forward in the study list; negative lag means moving backward. Opportunity correction matters because positions near a list boundary do not offer the same possible lags.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Lag-conditional response probability
text:
Follow one transition
The table takes the first two recalls from an eligible list. It shows the next item chosen, each available study position, and its lag from the preceding recall. This makes the denominator visible: every available alternative contributes an opportunity, while the chosen transition contributes an actual event.
Later transitions have fewer alternatives because previously recalled items are removed. The full calculation applies the library’s repeated-item conventions; the small illustration selects an unrepeated study list.


8 — Count the choices available for one transition
selected = np.logical_or.reduce([np.asarray(mask) for mask in trial_masks])
eligible = selected & ((np.asarray(data["recalls"]) > 0).sum(axis=1) >= 2)
unrepeated = np.array(
    [
        len(np.unique(items[items > 0])) == np.count_nonzero(items)
        for items in presentations
    ]
)
eligible_rows = np.flatnonzero(eligible & unrepeated)
if not len(eligible_rows):
    print(
        "No unrepeated list with two recalls to illustrate; transition-based summaries are undefined for this selection."
    )
else:
    row = int(eligible_rows[0])
    recall = np.asarray(data["recalls"])[row].astype(int)
    recall = recall[recall > 0]
    previous, chosen = recall[:2]
    available = np.flatnonzero(presentations[row] > 0) + 1
    available = available[available != previous]
    print(
        tabulate(
            {
                "Available study position": available,
                "Lag from previous recall": available - previous,
                "Chosen next": available == chosen,
            },
            headers="keys",
            floatfmt=".4g",
        )
    )
    print(f"Observed transition: {previous} to {chosen}; lag = {chosen - previous:+d}")

For each participant, counts of actual transitions are divided by available opportunities at each lag. The figure summarizes these participant curves with bootstrap intervals. An unavailable lag is undefined, not a zero-probability observation.

The illustration compares a chosen next item’s distance with the alternatives still available. Closer choices receive larger ranks, with midpoint ties. A score of 1 is the closest rank and 0 the farthest; with fewer than two alternatives the score is undefined.

title: Temporal organization scores
text:
Use this procedure to summarize temporal organization as a rank score for each participant and selection. It reads response files, evaluates chosen transitions relative to available alternatives, and saves a figure, participant scores and uncertainty summaries.
The rank method is part of the analysis definition. The historical lag-bin method remains the default; the optional item-midrank method treats equally distant items as separate alternatives with midpoint ties.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Temporal organization scores
text:
Illustrate an item-midrank transition
The table shows alternatives for the first transition in an eligible unrepeated list. The displayed score uses item midranks: each available item remains a separate alternative, and equally distant items receive midpoint ties. Higher scores favor nearer items; a transition with no alternative choice has no rank.
This illustration always uses item midranks. The aggregate default below is rank_method="lag_bins", the historical implementation that ranks available lag bins. Its handling of alternatives and ties differs. Set "item_midrank" only when that definition is intended and your study identities are unique.


8 — Rank one transition among its alternatives

unrepeated = np.array(
    [
        len(np.unique(items[items > 0])) == np.count_nonzero(items)
        for items in presentations
    ]
)
eligible_rows = np.flatnonzero(eligible & unrepeated)
if not len(eligible_rows):
    print(
        "No unrepeated list with two recalls to illustrate; transition-based summaries are undefined for this selection."
    )
else:
    row = int(eligible_rows[0])
    recall = np.asarray(data["recalls"])[row].astype(int)
    recall = recall[recall > 0]
    previous, chosen = recall[:2]
    available = np.flatnonzero(presentations[row] > 0) + 1
    available = available[available != previous]
    print(
        tabulate(

                "Lag from previous recall": available - previous,

    score = percentile_rank(jnp.asarray(abs(chosen - previous)), jnp.asarray(distances))

title: Exploring parameter effects
text:
Use this procedure to investigate what a fitted model does when selected parameters change. It loads saved baselines, simulates both the baseline and controlled changes on the same selected lists, and saves responses and comparisons.
This is a mechanism check: other parameters retain their fitted values. A parameter change may alter behavior while making the model fit the observations less well. To ask how well a different specification can fit after all free parameters adapt, use the fitting procedure instead.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: Exploring parameter effects

6 — Define participant-fit compatibility checks
def check_participant_fit(
    participant_record,
    reference_record,
    specification_keys,
    model_name,
):
    """Reject incompatible model specifications and pooled records."""
    if any(
        participant_record.get(key) != reference_record.get(key)
        for key in specification_keys
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"{model_name}: participant fits have incompatible model or input specifications."
        )
    participant_ids = participant_record["fits"]["subject"]
    if participant_record.get("pooled", False) or -1 in participant_ids:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{model_name}: directories must contain participant fits, not pooled fits."
        )




7 — Define participant-file combination
def combine_participant_fits(participant_records, data, model_name):
    """Combine compatible participant estimates without losing their identities."""
    subjects = np.asarray(data["subject"]).ravel()
    specification_keys = (
        "model_factory",
        "components",
        "simulation_function",
        "loss_function",
        "data_path",
        "fixed",
        "free",
        "embedding_path",
        "emotion_feature_path",
        "feature_column",
        "concat_features",
    )
    reference_record = participant_records[0]
    combined_parameters = combine_participant_parameters(
        [record["fits"] for record in participant_records]
    )
    selected_rows = set()
    for participant_record in participant_records:
        check_participant_fit(
            participant_record,
            reference_record,
            specification_keys,
            model_name,
        )
        participant_ids = participant_record["fits"]["subject"]
        if "selected_trial_indices" in participant_record:
            rows = participant_record["selected_trial_indices"]
            if not np.isin(subjects[rows], participant_ids).all():
                raise ValueError(
                    f"{model_name}: recorded observation rows belong to another participant."
                )
        else:
            mask = generate_trial_mask(
                data,
                participant_record.get(
                    "trial_query", participant_record.get("data_query")
                ),
            )
            rows = np.flatnonzero(
                np.asarray(mask) & np.isin(subjects, participant_ids)
            ).tolist()
        selected_rows.update(rows)
    combined_record = {
        key: reference_record[key]
        for key in specification_keys
        if key in reference_record
    }
    combined_record.update(
        name=model_name,
        label=reference_record.get("label", model_name),
        pooled=False,
        fits=combined_parameters,
        selected_trial_indices=sorted(selected_rows),
    )
    # Preserve boolean settings as recorded before the fitter's numeric conversion.
    combined_record["fixed"] = (
        reference_record.get("fit_configuration", {})
        .get("parameters", {})
        .get("fixed", reference_record["fixed"])
    )
    return combined_record

title: Simulating from saved fits
text:
Generate and save responses
Each repetition uses the selected experimental lists and keeps the original participant identity. simulation_seed controls random sampling; changing it asks for another realization of the same configured model.
The supplied fits use a simulator that forces observed recall lengths. Agreement in total recall or stopping is consequently imposed. To use a different simulator, set sim_alg_path and check that it answers your intended question. Saved responses have a JSON file of simulation settings; both files are used when checking whether a previous simulation can be reused.
With redo_sims=False, matching settings allow saved responses to be reused. Changes to data or model code in place are not detected: set redo_sims=True after those changes.


12 — Prepare participant parameters and simulation settings
simulation_inputs = {}
for model_name, fit_record in records.items():
    model_factory = construct_model(fit_record)
    features = load_features(fit_record)
    selected_trials = selections[model_name]
    is_pooled = fit_record.get("pooled", fit_record["fits"]["subject"] == [-1])
    participant_ids = jnp.unique(data["subject"].ravel()[selected_trials])
    subject_parameters = parameters_for_subjects(fit_record, participant_ids)
    configuration = {
        "fits": fit_record["fits"],
        "pooled": is_pooled,
        "jax_enable_x64": enable_x64,
        "jaxcmr_version": jaxcmr.__version__,
        "model_factory": fit_record["model_factory"],
        "components": fit_record["components"],
        "simulation_function": fit_record["simulation_function"],
        "data_path": data_source,
        "selected_trial_indices": np.flatnonzero(np.asarray(selected_trials)).tolist(),
        "embedding_path": fit_record.get("embedding_path", ""),
        "emotion_feature_path": fit_record.get("emotion_feature_path", ""),
        "feature_column": fit_record.get("feature_column", 6),
        "concat_features": fit_record.get("concat_features", False),
        "seed": simulation_seed,
        "experiment_count": experiment_count,
    }

    for key in ("embedding_path", "emotion_feature_path"):
        if configuration[key]:
            feature_path = resolve_project_path(configuration[key], root_path)
            configuration[key] = (feature_path.relative_to(root_path).as_posix()
                          if feature_path.is_relative_to(root_path) else str(feature_path))
    simulation_inputs[model_name] = {
        "model_factory": model_factory,
        "features": features,
        "parameters": subject_parameters,
        "trial_mask": selected_trials,
        "configuration": configuration,
    }




13 — Generate or reuse matching responses and save them
simulations = {}
for model_name, prepared in simulation_inputs.items():
    model_factory = prepared["model_factory"]
    features = prepared["features"]
    subject_parameters = prepared["parameters"]
    selected_trials = prepared["trial_mask"]
    configuration = prepared["configuration"]
    simulation_path = simulation_paths[model_name]
    metadata_path = simulation_path.with_suffix(".json")
    saved_metadata = (
        json.loads(metadata_path.read_text()) if metadata_path.exists() else {}
    )
    reuse_responses = (
        not redo_sims
        and simulation_path.exists()
        and metadata_path.exists()
        and simulation_metadata_matches(saved_metadata, configuration)
    )
    if reuse_responses:
        simulated = load_data(str(simulation_path))
        print("Loaded matching responses:", simulation_path)
    else:
        simulated = simulate_h5_from_h5(
            model_factory,
            data,
            features,
            subject_parameters,
            selected_trials,
            experiment_count=experiment_count,
            rng=jax.random.PRNGKey(simulation_seed),
            simulate_trial_fn=import_from_string(configuration["simulation_function"]),
        )
        simulation_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        save_dict_to_hdf5(simulated, str(simulation_path))
        metadata_path.write_text(
            json.dumps(
                {
                    **configuration,
                    "jaxcmr_version": jaxcmr.__version__,
                    "jax_version": jax.__version__,
                },
                indent=2,
            )
            + "\n"
        )
        print("Saved responses:", simulation_path)
    if filter_repeated_recalls:
        simulated = dict(simulated)
        simulated["recalls"] = repetition.filter_repeated_recalls(simulated["recalls"])
    simulations[model_name] = simulated
print(
    "simulation_paths =",
    {model_name: str(path) for model_name, path in simulation_paths.items()},
)

text:
Inspect behavioral summaries
The analysis configurations choose the behavioral comparisons. Their selection rules can differ from the fitting selection, so check which lists enter each display. Confidence intervals summarize participants; simulation repetitions are not additional independent participants.
Keep response files for subsequent analysis. You can inspect another behavior with an analysis template without simulating again.


14 — Prepare configured model and observation comparisons
comparison_groups = []
if (
    redo_figures
    and comparison_analysis_configs
    and any(not np.array_equal(mask, comparison_mask) for mask in selections.values())
):
    raise ValueError(
        "Shared comparison figures need matching selections; use separate jobs or disable comparison_analysis_configs."
    )

if redo_figures and simulations:
    observed = dict(data)
    if filter_repeated_recalls:
        observed["recalls"] = repetition.filter_repeated_recalls(observed["recalls"])
    datasets = [observed, *simulations.values()]
    names = ["Observed", *[display_labels[name] for name in simulations]]
    comparison_groups.append(
        {
            "analyses": comparison_analysis_configs,
            "datasets": datasets,
            "labels": names,
            "base_masks": [comparison_mask, *[None for _ in simulations]],
            "suffix": "",
        }
    )
    for dataset_index, (dataset, label) in enumerate(zip(datasets, names)):
        comparison_groups.append(
            {
                "analyses": single_analysis_configs,
                "datasets": [dataset],
                "labels": [label],
                "base_masks": [comparison_mask if dataset_index == 0 else None],
                "suffix": f"_single_{dataset_index}",
            }
        )




15 — Plot and save the configured benchmarks
for group in comparison_groups:
    panel_data = group["datasets"]
    analysis_configs = group["analyses"]
    curve_labels = group["labels"]
    base_masks = group["base_masks"]
    for figure, figure_suffix in iter_analysis_figures(
        panel_data, analysis_configs, curve_labels,
        base_masks=base_masks, trial_query=analysis_trial_query,
        confidence_level=confidence_level, figure_size=figure_size,
        suffix=group["suffix"],
    ):
        save_figure(
            str(figure_dir), figure_str, suffix=figure_suffix,
            formats=figure_formats, figure=figure,
        )

title: When recall ends
text:
Use this procedure to describe where recorded recall sequences end, either as a distribution of sequence lengths or as the probability of stopping after reaching each position. It reads observed or simulated responses and saves a figure for the selected modes and conditions.
Recording capacity limits what can be inferred from the final bin. Also check how simulated responses were produced: the supplied simulations impose observed recall lengths, so their agreement here does not demonstrate a model’s ability to predict stopping.
For input conventions, see the data guide.

title: When recall ends
text:
Configure this run
Choose response files and conditions. mode="simple" shows the proportion of sequences ending at each length; mode="conditional" divides endings by sequences that reached that position. Supply both in a list to inspect both views.
Overlaid datasets must have the same recording capacity. The complete-list filter applies to study lists; it does not remove the recall recording boundary.

Select the observations
select_conditions returns the masks and participant coverage without altering your data. Check the printed list and participant counts before interpreting the results. Queries are Python expressions evaluated with the dataset named data; replace the supplied condition codes with those in your data. trial_query overrides the list of trial_queries and uses selection_label.
With data_path set, the notebook reads that file and compares conditions. With data_path=None, data_paths and data_labels produce one panel per condition comparing datasets—even if the list contains just one file. Labels must correspond to the supplied selections and files.

text:
Interpret the stopping summaries
For a stored recall array of width K, the plotted lengths run from 0 to a final K−1+ bin. That final bin combines sequences ending there with sequences filling the recording capacity. The shaded region marks this limit; it cannot distinguish a voluntary stop from a recording cutoff.
The simple mode uses all selected sequences as its denominator. The conditional mode uses sequences that reached the relevant position. A position that was never reached has an undefined conditional probability. Participant summaries and bootstrap intervals are then plotted.


7 — Prepare the condition and dataset comparison panels
panels = comparison_panels(
    datasets, masks_by_dataset, input_labels, condition_labels,
    mode="conditions" if data_path is not None else "datasets",
    selection_label=selection_label,
)

modes = [mode] if isinstance(mode, str) else mode
mode_panels = []
for panel in panels:
    for display_mode in modes:
        mode_panels.append({**panel, "mode": display_mode})
panels = mode_panels




8 — Calculate, plot and save the selected comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(panels), 1, figsize=(8, 3.8 * len(panels)), squeeze=False)
for ax, panel in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
    panel_data = panel["datasets"]
    panel_masks = panel["trial_masks"]
    curve_labels = panel["labels"]
    title = panel["title"]
    display_mode = panel["mode"]
    plot_termination_probability(
        panel_data,
        panel_masks,
        mode=display_mode,
        labels=curve_labels,
        contrast_name=contrast_name,
        color_cycle=color_cycle,
        confidence_level=confidence_level,
        axis=ax,
    )
    title += f" — {display_mode}"
    widths = {dataset["recalls"].shape[1] for dataset in panel_data}
    if len(widths) != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            "Use matching recording capacities for overlaid terminal bins."
        )
    capacity = widths.pop()
    ax.set_xticks(
        np.arange(1, capacity + 1),
        [str(i) for i in range(capacity - 1)] + [f"{capacity - 1}+"],
    )
    ax.set_xlabel(f"Recorded recalls ({capacity - 1}+ = terminal recording bin)")
    ax.axvspan(capacity - 0.5, capacity + 0.5, color="grey", alpha=0.18)
    ax.set_title(title)

    if ax.get_legend_handles_labels()[1]:
        ax.legend(title=contrast_name)
    if ylim is not None:
        ax.set_ylim(ylim)
    if yticks is not None:
        ax.set_yticks(yticks)
save_figure(str(figure_dir), figure_str)
